question:
Summer in a modern city is not merely a matter of higher temperatures; it is a matter of unequal ones. Concrete, asphalt and glass absorb solar radiation through the day and release it slowly after dusk, so that densely built neighbourhoods can remain several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside long after the sun has set. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island effect, is aggravated by the waste heat of air-conditioners and vehicles, which makes the very devices meant to provide relief a part of the problem. For the poor, who often live in cramped, poorly ventilated housing with few trees nearby, the consequences are the most severe, and heat-related illness is a mounting burden on public health.

Planners have long regarded trees as an aesthetic luxury, the kind of embellishment that is funded in prosperous districts and quietly dropped from budgets elsewhere. Evidence now compels a reassessment. A mature tree cools its surroundings in two ways: its canopy intercepts sunlight before it reaches the ground, and its leaves release water vapour, which draws heat from the air much as perspiration cools the body. Studies in several cities have found that tree-lined streets can be markedly cooler than bare ones, and the benefits extend to lower electricity bills, cleaner air and reduced flooding, since roots and soil absorb rainwater that would otherwise overwhelm drains.

Yet planting trees is not the simple remedy it appears to be. Saplings need water, space and years of care before they offer meaningful shade, and many municipal drives record impressive planting figures but dismal survival rates. Species chosen for their rapid growth may prove unsuited to local conditions, while roots that buckle pavements invite complaints that lead to premature felling. The lesson is that the value of an urban forest lies less in the number of trees planted than in the number that survive to maturity. A city that treats its canopy as infrastructure, to be maintained and budgeted for like roads and sewers, will reap far greater rewards than one that treats it as decoration.

Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Air-conditioners and vehicles are the chief cause of the urban heat island effect, so trees are a better substitute for them.
Trees can help cool cities and bring other benefits, but they deliver these only when planted with care and kept alive over the long term.
The urban poor suffer most from heat, so tree planting should be confined to their neighbourhoods.
Municipal tree-planting drives have largely failed, and cities should spend on roads and sewers instead.

explanation:
नियम: Main idea / central idea वही विकल्प है जो पूरे passage का सार समेटे। गलत विकल्प प्रायः चार प्रकार के होते हैं: (i) Too narrow — केवल एक paragraph या एक detail की बात; (ii) Out of scope — passage में है ही नहीं; (iii) Extreme / distorted — always, never, only, sole, completely जैसे चरम शब्द या बात को तोड़-मरोड़कर पेश करना; (iv) Opposite — लेखक के मत के उलट।

यहाँ: सही उत्तर (B)। पूरे passage का सार: Para 2 में बताया गया है कि पेड़ गर्मी घटाते हैं (छाया, वाष्पन) और बिजली बिल, हवा, बाढ़ में भी लाभ देते हैं; Para 3 बताता है कि यह लाभ तभी मिलता है जब पेड़ जीवित रहें और उनकी देखभाल हो। यही विकल्प तीनों paragraphs को जोड़ता है।

अन्य विकल्प:
(A) — Distorted: AC और वाहनों की अपशिष्ट गर्मी केवल heat island को 'aggravate' करती है (para 1), उसे 'chief cause' नहीं कहा गया; पेड़ों को AC का विकल्प बताना passage में कहीं नहीं है।
(C) — Too narrow + distorted: गरीबों पर ज़्यादा असर केवल para 1 का एक ब्योरा है; पेड़ सिर्फ़ उनके इलाक़ों में लगें, ऐसा कहीं नहीं कहा गया।
(D) — Extreme / opposite: लेखक drives को असफल घोषित नहीं करता, केवल कहता है कि गिनती से ज़्यादा survival मायने रखता है; सड़क-सीवर का ज़िक्र सिर्फ़ रख-रखाव और बजट की सोच समझाने के लिए है।

pressing
chronic
diminishing

question:
In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay whose title, 'The Tragedy of the Commons', became a byword in the social sciences. Hardin asked his readers to picture a pasture open to all herders. Each herder, reasoning rationally, adds one more animal to his flock, since he alone enjoys the full gain from the extra animal while the cost of overgrazing is shared among everyone. The pasture, inevitably, is ruined. From this parable Hardin drew a bleak conclusion: shared resources are safe only when they are privatised or regulated from above, because ordinary users cannot be trusted to restrain themselves.

The argument was elegant, and it proved enormously influential among policymakers, who used it to justify transferring village forests and grazing lands to private owners or to state departments. But elegance is not the same as accuracy. The political scientist Elinor Ostrom, who shared the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2009, spent decades studying how communities actually manage shared resources, from alpine meadows in Switzerland to irrigation systems in Spain and forests in Japan. She found that many of these arrangements had endured for centuries, not because they were free of conflict, but because users had devised their own rules: who may take how much, who monitors the resource, and how offenders are penalised. Hardin, she observed, had described not a commons but an open-access free-for-all, in which no rules exist at all.

None of this means that commons are invariably well governed. Local rules can be unjust, excluding women or the landless from decisions, and they can crumble when outsiders, market pressures or sudden population growth overwhelm them. Ostrom's contribution was therefore not to romanticise the village but to widen the range of options. Between the market and the state, she argued, lies a third possibility: self-governance by those who depend on the resource, provided the rules are clear, the monitoring is local and the community has the authority to enforce its own decisions. Policymakers who overlook this possibility, she warned, risk dismantling working institutions in the name of repairing broken ones.

The passage is primarily concerned with:

options.text: challenging a once-influential theory by showing that communities can sustainably govern shared resources through rules of their own
proving that privatisation is the only dependable way of protecting shared resources
describing the life and academic achievements of Elinor Ostrom
showing that traditional village commons are free from injustice and conflict

explanation:
नियम: Main idea / central idea वही विकल्प है जो पूरे passage का सार समेटे। गलत विकल्प प्रायः चार प्रकार के होते हैं: (i) Too narrow — केवल एक paragraph या एक detail की बात; (ii) Out of scope — passage में है ही नहीं; (iii) Extreme / distorted — always, never, only, sole, completely जैसे चरम शब्द या बात को तोड़-मरोड़कर पेश करना; (iv) Opposite — लेखक के मत के उलट।

यहाँ: सही उत्तर (A)। Para 1 में Hardin का सिद्धांत, Para 2 में Ostrom के प्रमाणों से उसका खंडन, Para 3 में सीमाओं के साथ 'तीसरे रास्ते' (स्थानीय स्व-शासन) की बात। पूरा passage एक प्रभावशाली सिद्धांत को चुनौती देता है और बताता है कि समुदाय अपने नियमों से साझा संसाधन बचा सकते हैं।

अन्य विकल्प:
(B) — Opposite: यह Hardin का मत है, जिसे लेखक Ostrom के शोध के सहारे चुनौती देता है।
(C) — Too narrow: Ostrom का शोध मुख्य तर्क का साधन है, passage का विषय स्वयं Ostrom का जीवन या उपलब्धियाँ नहीं हैं।

In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay whose title, 'The Tragedy of the Commons', became a byword in the social sciences. Hardin asked his readers to picture a pasture open to all herders. Each herder, reasoning rationally, adds one more animal to his flock, since he alone enjoys the full gain from the extra animal while the cost of overgrazing is shared among everyone. The pasture, inevitably, is ruined. From this parable Hardin drew a bleak conclusion: shared resources are safe only when they are privatised or regulated from above, because ordinary users cannot be trusted to restrain themselves.

The argument was elegant, and it proved enormously influential among policymakers, who used it to justify transferring village forests and grazing lands to private owners or to state departments. But elegance is not the same as accuracy. The political scientist Elinor Ostrom, who shared the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2009, spent decades studying how communities actually manage shared resources, from alpine meadows in Switzerland to irrigation systems in Spain and forests in Japan. She found that many of these arrangements had endured for centuries, not because they were free of conflict, but because users had devised their own rules: who may take how much, who monitors the resource, and how offenders are penalised. Hardin, she observed, had described not a commons but an open-access free-for-all, in which no rules exist at all.

None of this means that commons are invariably well governed. Local rules can be unjust, excluding women or the landless from decisions, and they can crumble when outsiders, market pressures or sudden population growth overwhelm them. Ostrom's contribution was therefore not to romanticise the village but to widen the range of options. Between the market and the state, she argued, lies a third possibility: self-governance by those who depend on the resource, provided the rules are clear, the monitoring is local and the community has the authority to enforce its own decisions. Policymakers who overlook this possibility, she warned, risk dismantling working institutions in the name of repairing broken ones.

With which of the following statements would Elinor Ostrom most probably agree?

question:
Every translator eventually confronts a word that refuses to cross the border. The Portuguese saudade, the Japanese komorebi and the German Schadenfreude are routinely cited as untranslatable, and they are usually offered as proof that languages carve up experience in fundamentally different ways. The claim is seductive, but it needs to be handled with care. What these words resist is not translation but compression: the idea can be conveyed in English, though it may take a sentence rather than a single word. The real difficulty lies elsewhere, in the associations a word carries with it, the shared memories, the literary echoes and the faint social register that a native speaker absorbs without effort and a foreigner can almost never reproduce.

This is why poetry, which exploits such associations most heavily, is notoriously hard to translate, and why the translator's task is better understood as a negotiation than as a transfer. A literal rendering may preserve every dictionary meaning and yet lose the music, humour or irony of the original; a free rendering may capture the spirit and yet betray the author's choices. An old Italian proverb, traduttore, traditore, captures the dilemma in a pun: the translator is a traitor. The accusation is unfair, since a translator who never departs from the original is seldom faithful to it. Fidelity, in this view, is a matter of effect rather than of words, and demands that readers of the new language be moved, amused or disturbed in much the same manner as the readers of the first.

There is, besides, a consolation that rarely gets its due. Translation is not only a loss; it is also an act of creation that has repeatedly enriched the language receiving it. English acquired countless idioms, and even entire literary forms such as the sonnet, through the labours of translators who wrestled with texts that were never meant for it. A culture that stops translating does not preserve its purity; it merely grows poorer, deprived of the ideas that others have to offer.

Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: Untranslatable Words and the Differences Between Languages
The Treachery of Translators
How English Became the Language of Poetry
Beyond the Dictionary: The Difficulty and Worth of Translation

explanation:
नियम: Title वह होना चाहिए जो पूरे passage को समेटे और संक्षिप्त हो। बहुत narrow (केवल एक हिस्सा), out of scope (passage से बाहर) या लेखक के मत के उलट वाला title गलत होता है।

यहाँ: सही उत्तर (D)। Passage तीन बातें कहता है: (1) शब्दकोश से आगे की कठिनाई — जुड़ाव और प्रभाव (para 1-2); (2) निष्ठा का अर्थ प्रभाव में है (para 2); (3) अनुवाद का सृजनात्मक मूल्य (para 3)। 'The Difficulty and Worth of Translation' इन सबको समेटता है।

अन्य विकल्प:
(A) — Too narrow + contrary: यह केवल para 1 का हिस्सा है, और लेखक 'untranslatable' दावे को सावधानी से परखने को कहता है, उसका समर्थन नहीं करता।
(B) The Treachery of Translators — Opposite: लेखक 'translator is a traitor' वाले आरोप को स्पष्ट रूप से 'unfair' कहता है।
(C) — Out of scope: passage का केंद्र अनुवाद की कठिनाई और मूल्य है; अंग्रेज़ी का काव्य-भाषा बनना विषय नहीं है।

question:
Every translator eventually confronts a word that refuses to cross the border. The Portuguese saudade, the Japanese komorebi and the German Schadenfreude are routinely cited as untranslatable, and they are usually offered as proof that languages carve up experience in fundamentally different ways. The claim is seductive, but it needs to be handled with care. What these words resist is not translation but compression: the idea can be conveyed in English, though it may take a sentence rather than a single word. The real difficulty lies elsewhere, in the associations a word carries with it, the shared memories, the literary echoes and the faint social register that a native speaker absorbs without effort and a foreigner can almost never reproduce.

This is why poetry, which exploits such associations most heavily, is notoriously hard to translate, and why the translator's task is better understood as a negotiation than as a transfer. A literal rendering may preserve every dictionary meaning and yet lose the music, humour or irony of the original; a free rendering may capture the spirit and yet betray the author's choices. An old Italian proverb, traduttore, traditore, captures the dilemma in a pun: the translator is a traitor. The accusation is unfair, since a translator who never departs from the original is seldom faithful to it. Fidelity, in this view, is a matter of effect rather than of words, and demands that readers of the new language be moved, amused or disturbed in much the same manner as the readers of the first.

There is, besides, a consolation that rarely gets its due. Translation is not only a loss; it is also an act of creation that has repeatedly enriched the language receiving it. English acquired countless idioms, and even entire literary forms such as the sonnet, through the labours of translators who wrestled with texts that were never meant for it. A culture that stops translating does not preserve its purity; it merely grows poorer, deprived of the ideas that others have to offer.

options.text: prove that poetry cannot be translated without loss
illustrate the dangers of a free rendering
suggest that English culture has kept its purity by avoiding translation
show how translation can enrich the language that receives it

question:
It is easy to forget that time, in the sense of a single hour shared by everyone, is a recent invention. Until the nineteenth century, every town in Britain set its clocks by the sun, so that noon in Bristol arrived about ten minutes later than noon in London. The difference mattered little as long as travel was slow; a traveller on horseback could scarcely notice that he had crossed into a different hour. The railways changed everything. A timetable that listed arrivals and departures in dozens of local times was a recipe for confusion and, on single-track lines, for collision. In 1840 the Great Western Railway therefore adopted London time at all its stations, and within a few decades the entire country had followed.

The change did not arrive without protest. Many towns resented what they saw as an arbitrary imposition from the capital, and some clung to their local time for years, displaying clocks with two minute hands, one for local time and one for railway time. Critics complained that the railways were robbing communities of their natural rhythm, replacing the authority of the sun with the authority of a timetable. Their anxiety was not misplaced. Once everyone lived by the same clock, punctuality became a virtue, lateness a vice, and the working day something to be measured, bought and sold. The historian E. P. Thompson later argued that this new discipline of time was central to the making of the industrial workforce.

Yet the benefits were as real as the losses. Standard time made possible the coordination on which modern commerce, communication and eventually air travel depend. The United States, after a similar period of chaos in which railways used scores of different times, divided the continent into four zones in 1883. India, remarkably, adopted a single time for a country spanning almost thirty degrees of longitude, a decision that spares its citizens the confusion of zones but makes sunrise in the east noticeably earlier than the clock suggests. The history of standard time is thus a reminder that every convenience has a price, and that the price is usually paid by those least consulted when the bargain is struck.

Which of the following best summarises the passage?

options.text: The railways alone were responsible for the discipline of industrial labour in Britain.
Britain's towns successfully resisted London time, unlike those in the United States.
Standard time, introduced to serve the railways, brought coordination and commercial gains but at the cost of local autonomy and older rhythms of life.
A single national time, as in India, is preferable to the system of time zones used elsewhere.

We tend to regard a single, unbroken stretch of eight hours as the natural pattern of human sleep, and to treat any deviation from it as a disorder. History suggests otherwise. In a widely discussed study of pre-industrial Europe, the historian Roger Ekirch found hundreds of references, in diaries, court records and medical texts, to a practice of 'first sleep' and 'second sleep'. People went to bed soon after dusk, woke after a few hours, spent an hour or so awake, praying, chatting, tending the fire or visiting neighbours, and then slept again until morning. The interval was so ordinary that writers mentioned it without explanation, the way one would mention breakfast.

Ekirch argues that this pattern faded as artificial lighting spread, first in the streets of eighteenth-century cities and later in homes. Evenings grew longer and more productive, bedtimes moved later, and the two halves of the night fused into one. Laboratory work lends some support to the idea: when volunteers were kept in darkness for fourteen hours a day over several weeks, their sleep reportedly divided into two phases, separated by a spell of quiet wakefulness. Not every scholar is convinced, however. Sceptics note that the historical evidence, though plentiful, comes mainly from literate, urban or well-to-do sources, and that passing allusions to waking at night need not prove a universal custom. Studies of present-day communities without electricity, moreover, have often found people sleeping in a single consolidated block.

The debate, in the end, is less about the nights of our ancestors than about the anxieties of our own. Millions of people who wake in the small hours and cannot fall asleep again are told that something is wrong with them, and the fear of sleeplessness itself deepens the problem. If waking at night is a normal variant, as Ekirch's work implies, then the first step towards a remedy may be reassurance rather than medication. But the cautious reader should resist the temptation to treat an interesting hypothesis as a settled fact: the past is a poor guide to what the body requires, and what was customary is not thereby healthy.

We tend to regard a single, unbroken stretch of eight hours as the natural pattern of human sleep, and to treat any deviation from it as a disorder. History suggests otherwise. People went to bed soon after dusk, woke after a few hours, spent an hour or so awake, praying, chatting, tending the fire or visiting neighbours, and then slept again until morning. The interval was so ordinary that writers mentioned it without explanation, the way one would mention breakfast.

Ekirch argues that this pattern faded as artificial lighting spread, first in the streets of eighteenth-century cities and later in homes. Evenings grew longer and more productive, bedtimes moved later, and the two halves of the night fused into one. Laboratory work lends some support to the idea: when volunteers were kept in darkness for fourteen hours a day over several weeks, their sleep reportedly divided into two phases, separated by a spell of quiet wakefulness. Not every scholar is convinced, however. Sceptics note that the historical evidence, though plentiful, comes mainly from literate, urban or well-to-do sources, and that passing allusions to waking at night need not prove a universal custom. Studies of present-day communities without electricity, moreover, have often found people sleeping in a single consolidated block.

Millions of people who wake in the small hours and cannot fall asleep again are told that something is wrong with them, and the fear of sleeplessness itself deepens the problem. If waking at night is a normal variant, as Ekirch's work implies, then the first step towards a remedy may be reassurance rather than medication. But the cautious reader should resist the temptation to treat an interesting hypothesis as a settled fact: the past is a poor guide to what the body requires, and what was customary is not thereby healthy.
